abstract: The global ocean and land biosphere absorb roughly half of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. The temporal evolution of these sinks remains difficult to quantify owing to data sparsity. Leveraging 30+ years of atmospheric oxygen (O2) and CO2 observations, we find that the ocean carbon sink increased by 0.63 ± 0.19 petagrams of carbon per year per decade (Pg C year-1 decade-1) (a mean of 2.8 ± 0.4 Pg C year-1), accounting for 35% of fossil emissions between 1990 and 2019. The net land sink shows no robust trend (with a mean of 1.0 ± 0.5 Pg C year-1, accounting for 13% of fossil emissions), despite large decadal variability. These results challenge many process-based model simulations of the land and ocean sinks, questioning their ability to accurately predict future climate states.
hook: Air measurements show the ocean sink for CO2 grew since 1990 while the land sink stalled.

readout.label: Growth in ocean carbon sink, 1990 to 2019
readout.unit: Pg C per year per decade

summary: Thirty years of atmospheric oxygen and CO2 records let the authors separate ocean from land uptake, finding the ocean sink grew and took up 35% of fossil emissions in 1990 to 2019. The net land sink shows no clear trend. The results conflict with many process-based models, and the land estimate carries large uncertainty.
title: Atmospheric O2 reveals a strengthening ocean carbon sink and a stagnant net land sink since 1990.
